stories.body: Nvidia’s board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO less than two weeks after he resigned over an affair with a woman US officials accuse of working for Chinese intelligence. Trump said he personally pressed the board to bring Huang back and offered national security assurances. Nvidia shares rose more than 31%, adding nearly $1 trillion in market value, although they remained about 21% below their level a month earlier. Separately, the Commerce Department placed Singapore-based Megaspeed International, whose former executive is at the center of the allegations, and six other Southeast Asian firms on its export blacklist. Shipments of controlled US technology to those entities will now require licenses.
stories.headline: Nvidia reinstates Huang as shares surge; US blacklists firm linked to alleged spying

stories.body: NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance would defend against threats in space following German media reports that Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite within 60 days. The reports, citing unnamed military and intelligence sources, describe a satellite capable of disrupting or destroying other satellites, including communications and observation systems. Neither Rutte nor German Chancellor Friedrich Merz confirmed the intelligence, although German officials said they were taking it seriously. Russia’s embassy in Berlin rejected the allegations. Placing nuclear weapons in orbit would violate the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, to which Russia is a signatory.
stories.headline: NATO responds to unconfirmed reports of a Russian nuclear satellite launch

stories.body: Ukraine confirmed attacks on two Russian vessels at Benghazi in eastern Libya, saying seven naval drones launched from a mothership sank the corvette Merkury and struck the cargo ship MV Angara. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy released footage of the attack and said the cargo vessel was transporting weapons. The operation, roughly 1,500 miles from the Ukrainian front, extends Kyiv’s campaign against Russian military logistics well beyond the Black Sea. Authorities in eastern Libya lodged a complaint over the strikes and called for a UN investigation into allegations that Ukrainian forces were operating from western Libya. Russia supports eastern Libyan leader Khalifa Haftar and uses the region to support its military presence in Africa.
stories.headline: Ukraine claims naval drone attacks on Russian ships in Libya

stories.body: The UK imposed sanctions on five senior Myanmar military figures after the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during its 2017 military campaign. Fourteen countries acknowledged the ruling and called for compliance with international law. The court found that genocidal intent was the only reasonable inference from the evidence; Myanmar denied the allegations. The UK also announced plans for legislation to stop aviation fuel supplies and said it would raise the ruling at the UN Security Council. The campaign killed thousands and forced more than 700,000 Rohingya to flee, while continuing violence obstructs humanitarian relief.
stories.headline: UK sanctions Myanmar commanders after Rohingya genocide ruling

stories.body: Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory report indicators of environmental contamination across more than 99% of Gaza, warning that destroyed infrastructure and Israeli bombardment have left persistent threats to air, soil and water. Their analysis identifies risks from heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos and untreated sewage, with children and pregnant women especially vulnerable. All six wastewater treatment plants are out of operation. The findings rely heavily on satellite imagery and other remote evidence because destroyed laboratories and restrictions on equipment and access limit direct testing. Israel’s embassy in the UK disputed the report’s professional standards. The findings point to a cleanup and public health burden that could last decades.
stories.headline: Report warns Gaza’s environmental contamination could threaten health for decades

stories.body: The Justice Department acknowledged in court that Brian José Morales García, an Austin resident removed to Mexico in April, is a dual US–Mexican citizen. Born in Denver and raised in Mexico, he was detained after a Texas traffic stop despite telling officers that his birth certificate and Social Security card were at home. His lawsuit alleges that officials rebuffed attempts to provide citizenship documents and pressured him into signing expedited removal papers. The government disputes those allegations, argues that he left voluntarily and is seeking dismissal of his damages claim. Morales García was allowed back into the US on August 30 after officials reviewed evidence of his birthplace.
stories.headline: Justice Department acknowledges US citizenship of man removed to Mexico

stories.body: The final polls published before Spain’s November 29 election mostly project a comfortable parliamentary majority for PP and Vox, even as some show a close contest between PP and PSOE for first place. The 40dB survey for El País and Cadena SER puts PP at 31.8% and PSOE at 30.9%, with the right-wing bloc, including UPN, winning 187 seats against the 176 needed for a majority. Ipsos projects 190 seats for that bloc. The public CIS survey diverges sharply, placing PSOE at 34.4%, PP at 24.7% and Vox at 15.6%, without a seat projection. Its interviews ended November 17, before the televised Sánchez–Feijóo debate, limiting what it captures of the final campaign.
stories.headline: Final polls favor a PP–Vox majority, while CIS gives PSOE a wide lead

stories.body: Spanish long-haul airline Plus Ultra suspended all flights indefinitely on Monday, including its last remaining regular service to Venezuela, while negotiating with creditors through a pre-insolvency process. The carrier has not announced a restart date or detailed arrangements for passengers with existing tickets. Roughly 600 employees face uncertainty, with the company preparing a workforce reduction. Plus Ultra owes €53 million in pandemic rescue loans to the state holding company SEPI, which has recovered none of the principal and is demanding a viable continuity and repayment plan. The airline cites sharply higher fuel costs linked to the Iran war alongside operating losses; the original rescue is also under judicial investigation.
stories.headline: Plus Ultra suspends all flights as financial crisis threatens jobs and public loans

stories.body: Spain’s Supreme Court applied the amnesty to former Catalan president Carles Puigdemont and former ministers Toni Comín and Lluís Puig, definitively dismissing their case over the 2017 independence referendum. The ruling confirms investigating judge Pablo Llarena’s November 3 decision and rejects Vox’s requests to delay proceedings or seek another ruling from the EU’s top court. It follows European and Constitutional Court decisions that cleared the application of amnesty to the disputed misuse-of-public-funds charges. All members of the 2017 Catalan government are now covered by the amnesty. According to 3Cat, Puigdemont plans to return from Belgium after Spain’s November 29 election to give his return an institutional character.
stories.headline: Supreme Court grants Puigdemont amnesty and definitively closes referendum case
